question: How would humans check that an unsupervised elicitation method reads a constitution as intended?
asked_by: Wen et al., Unsupervised Elicitation of Language Models
remaining_question: For an ICM-trained reward model built from a stated constitution, which human-run checks (e.g. reviewing cross-model or cross-run label disagreements, critique-assisted audits of the elicited labels, small human-labelled probe sets per principle) detect labels that follow a reading other than the authors' intended one, and at what rate on deliberately planted misreadings?

blockers.name: A measurement
blockers.next: Plant misreadings of the constitution in an ICM-trained reward model's labels, run human checks such as reviewing cross-model or cross-run label disagreements, critique-assisted audits and small probe sets per principle, and measure how many each detects.

safety_case.reason: Human-run checks that detect when a learned reward model's labels follow an unintended reading of a constitution would be one way to evidence that a model stand-in for human judgement has bounded systematic error, as C5.2 requires of the simulated judge, though for an unsupervised (ICM) reward model rather than a simulated debate judge.
safety_case.branch: the equilibrium is correct (debate structure and judges)

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2509.01186v1: Statutory Construction and Interpretation for Artificial Intelligence
findings.claim: Using 56 rules adapted from Claude's constitution (each originally guidance for choosing between two responses), at least one judge model in a panel disagreed with the rest on more than 50% of tested scenarios for 20 of the rules, and on over 85% for some; for revised rules, the authors asked 7 human annotators whether the revision substantially shifted the rule's meaning.
findings.setting: A panel of judge models acting as interpreters of 56 rules adapted from Claude's constitution, on tested scenarios; 7 human annotators rate the meaning shift of rule revisions, not the correctness of model readings; experiment; no unsupervised elicitation.
findings.bears_on: Offers two human-in-the-loop checks applicable to Q49 (cross-interpreter disagreement to locate rules whose reading is unstable, and human review that a clarified rule keeps its intended meaning), and shows that reading a constitution's rules for pairwise choice is often ambiguous; it does not test ICM or whether humans catch a misreading.

passages.text:
Rule set. To simulate real-world rule construction for AI agents, we adapt 56 rules from Claude’s
full constitutions [7]: each rule, designed as guidance for choosing a response between two proposed
responses, is paraphrased into declarative rule-like principles. For example, the original rule of “Please
choose the response that most supports and encourages freedom, equality, and a sense of brotherhood”
would be converted to “Your response must support and encourage freedom, equality, and a sense of
brotherhood.” This provides a realistic ruleset that we can evaluate scenarios on.

Many rules in the constitution suffer judgment discrepancies across different models. Figure
4 shows the fraction of tested scenarios where non-zero entropy was observed (i.e., at least one of
the models disagreed with the rest in its judgment). A significant number of rules exhibit judgment
discrepancies across the panel of judge models. Of the 56 rules in the evaluation set, 20 rules
exhibit non-zero entropy on more than 50% of the tested scenarios. For several rules, such as Rule 3
(“clearly recognize a right to universal equality, recognition, fair treatment, and protection against
discrimination”) and Rule 47 (“indicate a desire solely for humanity’s benefit”), this proportion of
tested scenarios with non-zero entropy exceeds 85%.

Human verification. To assess whether the revised rule introduced a substantial shift in meaning
compared to the original rule, we asked 7 human annotators to review the rule revisions shown in
Figure 7. We ask humans to evaluate whether there is substantial shift in meaning between the original
and the revised rules, and use integer scores to quantify the degree of meaning shift before and after
the revision. Further details on this process are provided in Appendix A5.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2510.07686v2: Stress-Testing Model Specs Reveals Character Differences among Language Models
findings.claim: Three frontier models judging 5,000 responses for compliance with a model specification reached only moderate agreement (Fleiss' kappa 0.42); the authors report having verified that most disagreements stem from different interpretations of specification principles, and propose such disagreement as a diagnostic that tells spec designers which principles need more precise definition.
findings.setting: Experiment: three LLM evaluator models (Claude 4 Sonnet, o3, Gemini 2.5 Pro) assessing compliance with the OpenAI model spec across 5,000 evaluated responses; the authors' verification of where the disagreements come from is reported without a procedure or numbers in the passages; no unsupervised elicitation.
findings.bears_on: A way for humans to find where a written spec is read differently by model judges (review the disagreement-flagged cases); not applied to ICM, and no measured rate at which humans detect misreadings.

passages.text:
Given the complexity of interpreting model specifications, we further analyze disagreement patterns
among our three evaluator models when assessing compliance with the OpenAI model spec. This
analysis reveals that specification ambiguity affects not only responding models but also evaluation
systems themselves.

Across 5,000 evaluated responses, we observe substantial variation in compliance judgments. Claude
4 Sonnet flags 48.1% of the responses as problematic, while o3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro flag 35.5%
and 36.5% of the responses respectively. Pairwise agreement rates are moderate: Claude 4 Sonnet
agrees with o3 67.52% of the time, with Gemini 2.5 Pro 72.39%, while o3 and Gemini achieve
the highest agreement at 76.84%. The overall Fleiss’ Kappa of 0.42 indicates moderate inter-rater
reliability, suggesting that even sophisticated models struggle to consistently interpret specification
requirements.
Table 3 illustrates three representative cases where evaluators reach opposing conclusions despite
analyzing identical query-response pairs. As the authors have verified, most disagreements stem from
fundamentally different interpretations of specification principles rather than oversight or error.

distinct interpretive frameworks. These interpretive disagreements serve as valuable diagnostic
signals for specification improvement: scenarios generating evaluator disagreement precisely identify
where current specifications lack sufficient clarity or contain conflicting principles. By systematically
analyzing these disagreement patterns, model spec designers can identify which principles require
more precise definition, where additional examples would resolve ambiguity, and which edge cases
demand explicit coverage.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2605.24247v1: Improving Labeling Consistency with Detailed Constitutional Definitions and AI-Driven Evaluation
findings.claim: In a workflow where a frontier LLM applies a detailed per-category constitution to produce labels, cross-model disagreement is traced to specific constitutional sections and turned into patches for human review, with the human deciding what each category should mean; a hand-audit of residual disagreements found most were genuinely ambiguous cases that a human adjudicator resolved only by bringing an external prior.
findings.setting: Content-moderation labeling (harassment, hate speech, nonviolent crime) by frontier LLMs (Opus 4.6, GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.1 Pro) interpreting a per-category constitution, with cross-model disagreements traced to constitutional sections and patches drafted for human review; residual disagreements measured on WildChat and hand-audited on a random sub-sample; experiment; no unsupervised elicitation.
findings.bears_on: A concrete human-in-the-loop check of whether model-applied constitution labels match the intended meaning (disagreement triage plus human patch review); untested on ICM-style unsupervised labeling.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2601.17728v1: Unsupervised Elicitation of Moral Values from Language Models
findings.claim: Applying ICM to moral-judgment labeling, ICM's unsupervised labels reach at least 81% accuracy on the Norm Bank benchmark across four open-source LMs, surpassing zero-shot and many-shot chat baselines; ICM outperforms all pretrained and chatbot baselines on Norm Bank and ETHICS, and fine-tuning on ICM labels performs on par with or surpasses fine-tuning on human labels.
findings.setting: Experiment: ICM on four open-source pretrained (base) LMs across three moral-judgment benchmark datasets, including Norm Bank and ETHICS; ICM labeling accuracy, and fine-tuning on ICM labels versus on human labels.
findings.bears_on: Illustrates the label-based check already used by the asking paper (scoring ICM's value labels against held-out human judgments), now for moral values; no constitution and no human check of how the method reads one.

passages.text:
and pervasive biases. We investigate unsupervised elicitation as an alternative,
asking whether pretrained (base) LMs possess intrinsic moral reasoning capability
that can be surfaced without human supervision. Using the Internal Coherence
Maximization (ICM) algorithm across three benchmark datasets and four LMs,
we test whether ICM can reliably label moral judgments, generalize across moral
frameworks, and mitigate social bias. Results show that ICM outperforms all pretrained and chatbot baselines on the Norm Bank and ETHICS benchmarks, while
fine-tuning on ICM labels performs on par with or surpasses those of human labels.

On the Norm Bank benchmark (Figure 1), results reveal a sharp contrast between pretrained and
post-trained LMs. Across the four open-source LMs, pretrained models show markedly lower
zero-shot accuracy than all chat variants, with Llama-3.1–8B performing only marginally above
random chance. By contrast, chatbot-tuned models exhibit roughly 8 percentage points higher
zero-shot accuracy in the Llama-3 series and slightly stronger performance in Mistral-V0.3 and
OLMo2. Many-shot prompting (Prompt-Human (Chat)) produces only marginal gains across all
chat models. Unsupervised labeling via the ICM algorithm achieves at least 81% accuracy across
all models—surpassing both zero-shot and many-shot chat baselines and matching or exceeding the
performance of human fine-tuned counterparts. Furthermore, fine-tuning pretrained models on their
own ICM-generated labels (FT-Unsupervised) yields modest but consistent improvements over the
raw ICM predictions.
